links.note: Write the history of your family or village using sources of history at your disposal - the family-tree exercise is the one concept that asks the reader to gather family information and record where each fact came from.

Comparing historians to detectives is about the historian's method - gathering information from as many sources as they can, and deciding which source to trust when sources give contradictory information. Not the family-tree concept, which collects sources rather than weighing them.

The bundled date exercises - place 323 CE, 323 BCE, 100 CE, 1900 BCE, 2024 CE chronologically, King Chandragupta born 320 CE, Rani of Jhansi born 1828, turn 12,000 years ago into a date - are verbatim the third of the chapter's five closing projects, spanning timeline, century and BCE-to-CE arithmetic together rather than any one of them.
Plan a visit to a nearby museum with prior research on its exhibits, keep notes and write a brief report on what was unexpected, interesting or fun - verbatim the fourth closing project.

Invite an archaeologist or historian to your school to speak on the history of your region and why it is important to know it - verbatim the fifth closing project, not the concept that defines what an archaeologist does.

The academic discipline that studies the human past is History - this is the chapter's opening definition of history as the study of the human past, distinguished here from geography, sociology and anthropology.
A geologist studies the physical features of the Earth - soil, stones, hills and mountains - which is the first of the four experts introduced in this concept.

A palaeontologist studies the preserved remains and traces of ancient plants, animals and humans as fossils - the second of the four experts, and the distractors are the other three from the same list.
The expert who studies the human past by excavating and analysing material remains people left behind is the archaeologist - the fourth of the four experts defined here.

A time line is the visual representation showing a sequence of dates and important events over a period - the definition this concept opens with, rejected against the century/millennium units concept because nothing is being counted here.
A century is a period of one hundred years - one of the two longer units of time supplied by the DON'T MISS OUT box, not the era or calendar concept.
A millennium is any period of one thousand years, with a decade and a century as the distractors - all three units come from this concept's box.

A source of history is a place, person, text or object from which we gather information about a past event - this concept carries that exact definition, which the family-tree exercise then puts to work.

Monuments and mounds classified as archaeological structures is a question about the figure of the main sources of history, which sits in this concept; the archaeologist concept defines the digger, not the categories of source.

Tools, pots, figurines and pottery found through site excavations is the archaeologist's own activity as this concept lists it - tools, pots, beads, figurines, toys, bones - rather than a source-category question.
Folklore and genealogical records placed under spoken oral sources tests the source-category figure this concept holds, against literary, artistic and excavated as distractors.
Travelogues by foreign visitors as foreign literary accounts is again the main-sources-of-history categories brought together in this concept's closing figure.

Paintings, sculptures and carved panels as artistic sources - the artistic branch of the source-category figure, not the rock-painting concept, since these are sources being classified rather than early human art.

The historian's main task is to gather and consult as many sources as they can find - the sentence this concept opens with, and its distractors (accept one source, ignore contradictory data) are the failures it warns against.
Modern humans Homo sapiens have walked the planet about 300,000 years - this concept's opening figure, correctly linked already.

The control of fire belongs to this concept - these groups used fire and began making improved stone axes and blades - and not to the Homo sapiens concept, whose content is the timescale and the band.
Aspects of early human life visibly depicted in colourful rock paintings found in hundreds of caves - the rock-painting material sits squarely in this concept.
The last great Ice Age ending around 12,000 years ago and changing living conditions - this concept states that span (over 100,000 to around 12,000 years ago) and the improvement that followed.
Besides cultivating cereals and grains, settled communities domesticated animals such as cattle and goats - the paired sentence in this concept.

Early agricultural communities settled near rivers for water and more fertile soil - this concept gives both reasons explicitly, which is what separates the correct option from easy defence or wild game.
A hamlet is a small settlement or small village - glossed in this concept, where hamlets grow into sizeable villages and some into small towns.
An era is a distinct period of time often marked by a significant event - the gloss this concept carries, where the birth of an important person or a ruler's reign marks a new era.
The years before the conventional date of Jesus' birth are Before Common Era - this concept's BCE half, not the Gregorian calendar concept where era is merely glossed.

Pairing each study field with its subject - geology, palaeontology, anthropology, archaeology with excavated material remains as the correct match - is exactly the four-expert list this concept sets out.
A chart showing the reigns of Roman emperors in order is a simple time line - this concept's point that a timeline shows the order in which events take place, applied to a new case.

Old photographs and relatives' memories as valid sources for a familial past is the follow-up question of this concept's family-tree exercise, which names photographs, diaries, cards and memories. Already linked and correct.

Spotting that Oral paired with rock paintings is the incorrect match, against archaeological coins, literary travelogues and artistic temple sculptures, tests the source-category figure this concept brings together.

The surviving fragment is about first using iron for tools, and this concept is the only one that dates metal - copper first and iron later, helping make durable tools. The stem's numbered statements 1 and 2 are missing from the item text.
Early humans lived in bands or groups to help each other, constantly seeking shelter and food - this concept's sentence, which is why better shelter and food beats artistic expression or trade.
The period 2001 CE to 2100 CE is the 21st century CE - this concept states that span for the current century exactly.
Welfare glossed as health, prosperity and well-being appears only in this concept, where chieftains were responsible for the well-being of the people.
Agriculture changed food-getting because people produced their own food instead of hunting and gathering - the settling-down and cultivating turn this concept narrates.
Everything archaeologists study EXCEPT future climate predictions - the correct exclusion is judged against this concept's list of tools, remains of houses and burnt grains.
Pottery as a new technology for making pots and other clay objects appears in this concept alongside metal; better food storage is the consequence being asked for.
The shift from hunting and gathering to agriculture enabling settled life is this concept's central claim - living conditions improved and people started settling down and cultivating cereals.

Early humans learned to make simple ornaments such as stone or shell beads and pendants made of animal teeth, and sometimes exchanged them - this concept's closing detail, which is what makes the trade and symbolic reason true.
The incorrect pair is Millennium as a period of 10 years; the decision turns on the millennium and century lengths this concept supplies, while CE and BCE appear only as correct distractors.

Reading stone tools in the lowest layer, pottery and grains above, iron implements on top as a sequence of different periods is the archaeologist's method as this concept defines it - studying the past by digging up remains preserved within layers of soil or rocks.
Chipped stone as the material for cutting tools like axes and blades - this concept names improved stone axes and blades and arrowheads, and rules out bronze, clay and wood.
Metallurgy starting with copper advancing beyond stone because metal tools were more durable - this concept says copper first and iron later helped make durable tools, in those words.

Ancient Roman coins in a museum as archaeological sources - this concept opens on old coins, books, clothes, jewellery and utensils as objects that carry information, and holds the source-category figure the options draw on.
The visible statement, that a millennium is shorter than a century, is judged against this concept's units - 1,000 years against 100. The item's other numbered statements are missing from the stem.
The period when humans primarily used stone for making tools - this concept is the chapter's account of stone tool-making, improved stone axes, blades and arrowheads.
Agriculture as a turning point giving more stable food supplies - with more food available these communities grew in size and number, which is this concept's sentence.

Figurines and burial goods as the objects that reveal early beliefs - this concept is the one that says early ancestors had beliefs about natural elements and possibly some notion of afterlife, the hedge the question depends on.
Epigraphy as the study of ancient inscriptions - epigraphists are named only in this concept's list of people who contribute to historical sources.

A soldier's wartime diary classified as a primary literary source is a source-category judgement, which belongs with the figure of the main sources of history in this concept rather than with the historian's weighing of them.
The study of the human past is History - the bare definition this concept states right after the earliest-memory exercise.
Geologists study the physical features of the Earth like soil and mountains - the first expert in this concept's four.
Fossils as impressions or preserved remains of ancient plants and animals found within layers of rock - the term is glossed in this concept beside the palaeontologist.
Archaeologists study past human life by digging up remains like tools and pottery - this concept's definition of the archaeologist.
CE stands for Common Era - this concept explains that AD was replaced by Common Era or CE across the world.
